system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2176-11-10 01:52:00 to 2176-11-15 19:25:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with diffuse abdominal and back pain, mild shortness of breath, and suspected fever. She had recently been hospitalized for decompensated diastolic heart failure and was not taking her furosemide at home. On admission, she had signs of urinary tract infection with a positive urinalysis, and was started on IV antibiotics, later narrowed to oral Bactrim. Pulmonary edema was confirmed on imaging, and she was treated with IV furosemide before transitioning to oral therapy. Her Foley catheter was changed to reduce infection risk. A CT scan showed no acute abdominal process but confirmed cirrhotic liver changes. Lower extremity ultrasound ruled out DVT. She improved clinically and was discharged on oral furosemide and a 7-day course of Bactrim, with instructions to monitor daily weight and follow up with her providers.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Acute on chronic diastolic (congestive) heart failure
Unspecified cirrhosis of liver
Morbid (severe) obesity due to excess calories
Asymptomatic human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] infection status
Unspecified viral hepatitis B without hepatic coma
Unspecified viral hepatitis C without hepatic coma
Opioid dependence, in remission

Brief Hospital Course:
___ with hx of obesity, dCHF, HIV on HAART, HBV/HCV, IVDU on 
dilaudid/methadone, b/l nephrolithiasis with recurrent VRE UTIs 
with chronic indwelling foley catheter who presents with 
multiple complaints attributed to sepsis, ultimately left 
against medical advice. 

#Sepsis: 
#E coli Bacteremia:
On admission the patient was hypotensive, with acute renal 
failure and a lactate of 7.  There was inital concern for UTI 
vs. Pneumonia. She was started on Linezolid (has allergy to 
vancomycin) and Zosyn in the ED.  While in the ICU, blood 
pressures as low as 60/30's were recorded, but were thought 
unreliable given her morbid obesity and difficulty finding an 
appropriate sized cuff; pulses at the wrist were strong during 
these episodes.  Eventually, blood pressures were taken off the 
wrist and ankles and found to be in the ___ consistently. 
She was transferred to the floor in stable condition, with blood 
culture growing E coli and urine culture growing mixed flora. 
For transaminitis (see below) with gram-negative bacteremia, 
patient was recommended to have CT abdomen, but she declined to 
undergo this test and instead left against medical advice. She 
was transitioned from IV Zosyn to empiric Bactrim to complete 
14d after insisting that she leave the hospital. 

#Acute Kidney Injury: 
Likely pre-renal from sepsis with accompanying ATN from 
prolonged poor perfusion. Cr peaked at 3.3, was 1.1 on 
discharge. 

#Transaminitis:
Given history of HBV/HCV, cirrhosis was suspected with 
consistent radiographic findings on RUQ U/S, perhaps with 
superimposed shock liver from sepsis. There was some concern for 
intra-abdominal source of infection in setting of gram-negative 
bacteremia for which CT abdomen was recommended, but patient 
adamantly declined and left AMA instead. 

#Acute on Chronic Diastolic Heart failure: 
Patient with history of diastolic CHF requiring significant 
diuresis in the past. proBNP on admission significantly elevated 
compared to most recent in-system values. ECHO was obtained, of 
limited quality given body habitus. She was not diuresed in the 
setting of sepsis and ___ she may have had post-ATN diuresis as 
she was cumulatively -14L negative from her floor stay. For 
continued supplemental O2 requirement (likely multifactorial 
from OHS, atelectasis, though could also have had component of 
pulmonary edema), she was recommended to stay, but decided to 
leave against medical advise. Discharge weight was 167.38kg.

#Hyponatremia/Hypochloremia:
Likely due to poor solute intake in the setting of sepsis. There 
was come concern for adrenal insufficiency from chronic narcotic 
use or interaction of inhaled cortiocsteriods and her Stribild, 
but her serum electrolytes normalized with improvement in her 
oral intake. 

#Thrombocytopenia:
In setting of possible cirrhosis and sepsis. Platelet count on 
discharge was 85.

#Hypoxemia:
#Hx Asthma:
Likely multifactorial from acute on chronic diastolic heart 
failure, probable obesity hypoventilation syndrome, atelectasis. 
Patient has history of asthma, which was not active this stay. 

#HIV: 
Held HAART in the setting ___ and resumed once ___ resolved.

#Chronic Pain Syndrome: 
On methadone at home. Held at admission and resumed once acute 
renal failure resolved.

#Goals of Care: 
#AMA Discharge: 
Patient was adamant to floor providers that she did not want 
invasive resuscitation, blood products or sedation. On the day 
of discharge, she declined further evaluation for her 
transaminitis, source of sepsis and hypoxemia despite being 
counseled on the risks of leaving including injury and death, 
which she was able to repeat back. She was oriented and in a 
clear (if frustrated) state of mind on the day of discharge. She 
understood to return if her condition worsened.

discharge. 
#Depression: Held duloxetine while receiving linezolid, 
restarted once linezolid was stopped. 
#Migraine: Continued home sumatriptan once off linezolid.

___ with hx of obesity, dCHF, HIV on HAART, HBV/HCV, IVDU on 
dilaudid/methadone, b/l nephrolithiasis with recurrent VRE UTIs 
with chronic indwelling foley catheter who presents with 
multiple complaints attributed to sepsis, ultimately left 
against medical advice. 

#Sepsis: 
#E coli Bacteremia:
On admission the patient was hypotensive, with acute renal 
failure and a lactate of 7.  There was inital concern for UTI 
vs. Pneumonia. She was started on Linezolid (has allergy to 
vancomycin) and Zosyn in the ED.  While in the ICU, blood 
pressures as low as 60/30's were recorded, but were thought 
unreliable given her morbid obesity and difficulty finding an 
appropriate sized cuff; pulses at the wrist were strong during 
these episodes.  Eventually, blood pressures were taken off the 
wrist and ankles and found to be in the ___ consistently. 
She was transferred to the floor in stable condition, with blood 
culture growing E coli and urine culture growing mixed flora. 
For transaminitis (see below) with gram-negative bacteremia, 
patient was recommended to have CT abdomen, but she declined to 
undergo this test and instead left against medical advice. She 
was transitioned from IV Zosyn to empiric Bactrim to complete 
14d after insisting that she leave the hospital. 

#Acute Kidney Injury: 
Likely pre-renal from sepsis with accompanying ATN from 
prolonged poor perfusion. Cr peaked at 3.3, was 1.1 on 
discharge. 

#Transaminitis:
Given history of HBV/HCV, cirrhosis was suspected with 
consistent radiographic findings on RUQ U/S, perhaps with 
superimposed shock liver from sepsis. There was some concern for 
intra-abdominal source of infection in setting of gram-negative 
bacteremia for which CT abdomen was recommended, but patient 
adamantly declined and left AMA instead. 

#Acute on Chronic Diastolic Heart failure: 
Patient with history of diastolic CHF requiring significant 
diuresis in the past. proBNP on admission significantly elevated 
compared to most recent in-system values. ECHO was obtained, of 
limited quality given body habitus. She was not diuresed in the 
setting of sepsis and ___ she may have had post-ATN diuresis as 
she was cumulatively -14L negative from her floor stay. For 
continued supplemental O2 requirement (likely multifactorial 
from OHS, atelectasis, though could also have had component of 
pulmonary edema), she was recommended to stay, but decided to 
leave against medical advise. Discharge weight was 167.38kg.

#Hyponatremia/Hypochloremia:
Likely due to poor solute intake in the setting of sepsis. There 
was come concern for adrenal insufficiency from chronic narcotic 
use or interaction of inhaled cortiocsteriods and her Stribild, 
but her serum electrolytes normalized with improvement in her 
oral intake. 

#Thrombocytopenia:
In setting of possible cirrhosis and sepsis. Platelet count on 
discharge was 85.

#Hypoxemia:
#Hx Asthma:
Likely multifactorial from acute on chronic diastolic heart 
failure, probable obesity hypoventilation syndrome, atelectasis. 
Patient has history of asthma, which was not active this stay. 

#HIV: 
Held HAART in the setting ___ and resumed once ___ resolved.

#Chronic Pain Syndrome: 
On methadone at home. Held at admission and resumed once acute 
renal failure resolved.

#Goals of Care: 
#AMA Discharge: 
Patient was adamant to floor providers that she did not want 
invasive resuscitation, blood products or sedation. On the day 
of discharge, she declined further evaluation for her 
transaminitis, source of sepsis and hypoxemia despite being 
counseled on the risks of leaving including injury and death, 
which she was able to repeat back. She was oriented and in a 
clear (if frustrated) state of mind on the day of discharge. She 
understood to return if her condition worsened.

restarted once linezolid was stopped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling really weak, nauseous, throwing up, and I’ve had diarrhea. I can’t catch my breath like I used to. I think I might have pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s important. You also mentioned chills and fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been hot and cold, and my head’s been pounding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your vitals and labs. Your blood pressure dropped after arrival, and your white blood cell count is very high. That means your body is fighting a serious infection—sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sepsis? That sounds bad. Where’s the infection coming from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. Could be your lungs or your urinary tract. Your urine showed signs of infection, but we couldn’t get a clear culture because of contamination.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have a Foley catheter at home. Could that be it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Chronic catheters are a common source. We already changed it to reduce infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started you on two antibiotics—Zosyn and Linezolid—because of your allergies. We’ll adjust once we know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be intubated. I’m DNR. I’ve said that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for telling me. We’ve documented that. You won’t be intubated unless you change your mind. We’ll focus on comfort and treating the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I just want to get better without machines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back—E. coli is growing. That confirms a bloodstream infection, likely from your urinary tract.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: E. coli? Like food poisoning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same bacteria, but here it’s from your catheter. The good news is it’s sensitive to the antibiotics we’re using.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m on the right meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll keep IV antibiotics for now. Your kidneys are stressed—creatinine is high—so we’re watching that closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your kidneys. No blockage. That’s good. But we also did a liver ultrasound because your liver enzymes are up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My liver? I have hepatitis B and C.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and the ultrasound shows changes consistent with cirrhosis. We’re worried the infection might be coming from your abdomen, not just the catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what do you want to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend a CT scan of your abdomen to check for any abscess or other source. It’s important to make sure we’re treating the right problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want more tests. I just want to go home when I’m better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But without the scan, we can’t rule out a serious source. It could make you worse if we miss it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show improvement. White count is coming down, and your kidney function is starting to recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? Can I go soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re improving, yes. But we still recommend the CT scan and a few more days of monitoring, especially your breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m breathing okay now. I don’t want to stay longer than I have to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve held off on the CT because you declined. Your infection markers are better. We’re switching from IV to oral antibiotics—Bactrim—for 14 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home with pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d prefer you stay until you’re off oxygen and the CT is done. But if you insist on leaving, we can arrange it with oral antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand the risks. I want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look much better. Creatinine is down to 1.1, and your sodium is improving. Platelets are still low, likely from liver disease and infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my kidneys are okay now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’re recovering. Your liver enzymes are still high, but that may be from the infection. We still don’t know if there’s an abdominal source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know you want me to stay, but I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve spent time with social work and nursing. You’ll go home with services. You’ll finish 14 days of Bactrim.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your regular meds are restarted—methadone, furosemide, Stribild, gabapentin, everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I need my pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: your breathing is better on 2 liters oxygen. We still recommend staying until you’re off oxygen, but you’re clear to leave AMA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: AMA? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Against Medical Advice. It means we think it’s safer to stay, but you’re choosing to leave now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ll come back if I feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Watch for fever, trouble breathing, or confusion. And please consider talking to your doctor about your catheter—it’s a recurring infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send your discharge instructions and prescriptions. A nurse will help you get home safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your urine test today showed a new large stone in your left kidney. Follow up with urology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. More problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s a lot. But you’ve made real progress. Just keep up with your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in to assist you shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch with your primary team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with sepsis, presenting with weakness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and shortness of breath. Initial labs showed severe infection with E. coli bacteremia, acute kidney injury, and transaminitis. She was treated with IV antibiotics, later transitioned to oral Bactrim. Her condition improved, with normalization of kidney function and reduction in infection markers. A liver ultrasound suggested cirrhosis, and a new left renal stone was identified. Despite recommendations for a CT scan and continued oxygen monitoring, the patient chose to be discharged against medical advice. She was sent home with a full medication regimen, including a 14-day antibiotic course, and instructions to follow up with her providers.
